docs.title: Tutorial
docs.text: A scenario describes a network, its traffic, failure policies and an ordered workflow. Preparation turns it into one read-only graph with one bandwidth unit q, and a run returns typed results (Scenario, preparation and run).

docs.title: Write a scenario
docs.text:
Save this as example.yaml:

seed: 42
network:
  nodes: {A: {}, B: {}, C: {}}
  links:
    - {source: A, target: B, capacity: 10, cost: 1}
    - {source: B, target: C, capacity: 10, cost: 2}
failures:
  random_link:
    modes:
      - weight: 1
        rules:
          - {scope: link, mode: choice, count: 1}
demands:
  traffic:
    - {source: ^A$, target: ^C$, volume: 4, preset: SHORTEST_PATHS_ECMP}
workflow:
  - type: MaxFlow
    name: ideal_capacity
    source: ^A$
    target: ^C$
    preset: TE_MAXFLOW_UNLIM
    outputs: {min_cut: true, cost_distribution: true}
  - type: MaximumSupportedDemand
    name: supported_load
    demand_set: traffic
  - type: TrafficMatrixPlacement
    name: under_failures
    demand_set: traffic
    alpha_from_step: supported_load
    failure_policy: random_link
    iterations: 20

Each physical link carries traffic in both directions, each with its full capacity (Links, directions and what is enabled). Costs are positive integers (link keys). Volumes and capacities are physical amounts; native bandwidth results are whole units of q, which preparation chooses (Units and the resolution q).

seed makes the random failure draws repeatable (Seeds).

What the other keys mean:

  • failures declares a failure policy: here, one random link fails per draw (Failures: patterns, cases and states; failures).
  • A preset names a model: SHORTEST_PATHS_ECMP splits whole units equally among equal-cost next hops at each router; TE_MAXFLOW_UNLIM asks for the largest flow (Routing models and admission).
  • outputs asks for optional results: here the minimum cut and the cost report (Output selection).
  • MaximumSupportedDemand searches for the largest multiplier alpha of the demand volumes that the network carries in full, until the gap between a feasible and an infeasible alpha is at most alpha_tolerance, 0.01 by default (Maximum supported demand; MaximumSupportedDemand).
  • alpha_from_step places the demands at the multiplier an earlier MSD step found (Demands: how traffic enters; TrafficMatrixPlacement).
  • failure_policy and iterations run that placement over 20 failure draws (Keys common to analysis steps).

docs.title: Run and inspect
docs.text:
ngraph inspect example.yaml
ngraph run example.yaml --output results/
ngraph run example.yaml --stdout --no-results
ngraph run example.yaml --profile --output results/

run writes results/example.results.json. --stdout emits pure JSON, and --profile reports where the run spends its time; diagnostic and step-profile reports go to stderr. The output file is replaced after complete encoding succeeds (Command Line).

docs.title: Read results
docs.text:
The document has metadata, units_report and an ordered steps array. Each step records its normalized question (what it asked) and typed result. The units_report holds q and the run's precision (Results and their units); each failure case's states.converged.totals holds the placement's totals in the converged state (Failures: patterns, cases and states, Demands: how traffic enters).

jq '.steps[] | select(.name == "supported_load") | .result.alpha_feasible.value' results/example.results.json

2.5

MSD reports its largest tested feasible alpha and every probe it made; the placement step records that it used that alpha (Maximum supported demand). alpha_feasible is an exact fraction with its value, numerator and denominator; .value prints the number.

jq -c '.units_report.q as $q | .steps[] | select(.name == "under_failures") | .result.cases[]
  | {case: .case.id, occurrences: .case.occurrences,
     requested: (.states.converged.totals.reference_request_units * $q),
     delivered: (.states.converged.totals.delivered_units * $q)}' results/example.results.json

{"case":"baseline","occurrences":0,"requested":10,"delivered":10}
{"case":"failure-000001","occurrences":11,"requested":10,"delivered":0}
{"case":"failure-000002","occurrences":9,"requested":10,"delivered":0}

Totals are in units of q, so the command multiplies them by q for physical bandwidth (Units and the resolution q). The intact chain has physical capacity 10, cut at A→B, and route cost 3. Either single-link failure disconnects A from C. The 20 draws therefore collapse into at most two failure patterns, plus the baseline. occurrences sum to 20; the baseline is not an extra trial (Failures: patterns, cases and states).

Every case asks the same request, so the worst case is the one that delivers least, here either failure (Failures: patterns, cases and states); what a case does not deliver was not admitted or was dropped (Demands: how traffic enters).

To export one step, add --keys under_failures: the whole workflow still runs, and the step keeps its execution order 2 (Filtering Results by Step Names).

docs.title: Use Python
docs.text:
from pathlib import Path
from ngraph import Scenario, prepare, run, write_json

scenario = Scenario.from_yaml(Path("example.yaml").read_text())
prepared = prepare(scenario)
result = run(prepared)
for step in result.steps:
    print(step.name, step.step_type)
with open("python-results.json", "w") as destination:
    write_json(result, destination)

ideal_capacity MaxFlow
supported_load MaximumSupportedDemand
under_failures TrafficMatrixPlacement

Results belong to the returned run; topology edits after prepare need a new preparation (Scenario, preparation and run). Library users can prepare selected demand sets and call capacity, place, paths, edge_sensitivity or maximum_supported_demand directly with typed queries (Python API).

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: Scenario.from_yaml refuses invalid input with ValueError, whose message starts with the field's path and value. A constructor refuses an invalid field with ValueError naming the field. Each entry's Raises section lists its other cases.

docs.title: Python API
docs.text: The Python API takes typed records and queries; YAML is parsed into the same records. This guide shows the library by task; the generated reference lists every public name, and Scenario YAML, Workflow Steps and Command Line describe the file and command boundaries.

docs.title: Prepare and query
docs.text:
from ngraph import (
    CapacityQuery, Link, Network, Node, Scenario, Selector, UnitsSettings,
    capacity, prepare,
)

network = Network()
for name in ("A", "B", "C"):
    network.add_node(Node(name))
network.add_link(Link("A", "B", capacity=10, cost=1))
network.add_link(Link("B", "C", capacity=5, cost=2))
prepared = prepare(Scenario(network, units=UnitsSettings(resolution=1)))
result = capacity(prepared, CapacityQuery(Selector("^A$"), Selector("^C$")))
row = result.cases[0].states["converged"].rows[0]
assert row.result.delivered == 5
assert prepared.topology.q == 1

Network keeps editable dicts of immutable records. prepare resolves the selected demand sets, builds one native graph and returns PreparedScenario; it does not change its input. Library callers name needed demand sets with prepare(scenario, demand_sets=("traffic",)); workflow-referenced sets are included automatically.

PreparedScenario holds the read-only scenario view, its topology, the bound demand_sets and the preparation's units_report. PreparedTopology holds the graph and its labels: graph, physical node names, read-only node-name and physical-link mappings, edge_refs (each engine edge's directed link or pool attachment, in edge order), disabled (the engine's eligibility mask of what the scenario disables), q (the bandwidth unit; Units and the resolution q) and pool_heads (each finite TE ingress pool's synthetic head node; Tunnels and TE ingress pools). Every analysis takes the prepared scenario, holds it as prepared and uses the preparation's units_report, with controller weight approximations added for a later-bound demand set. A physical link has two native directions; DirectedLink(link, direction) identifies one. Returned results stay readable after the scenario and the prepared scenario are deleted. The prepared view is read-only, and later edits need a new preparation (Scenario, preparation and run). The examples on this page fix q to 1, so that units equal physical bandwidth; for amounts this small that misses the default precision target, and their units reports say so (Precision and the choice of q).

docs.title: Native models and capacity
docs.text:
CapacityQuery defaults to uncapped, lossless optimized traffic engineering. mode="combine" asks one source-set/destination-set question; "pairwise" asks one question per source-group and target-group pair, in canonical order (groups sorted by label). Selector(group_by="name", path="^source") makes one group per matching node. Overlapping source and target groups are refused, except a pair that is one and the same node, which has its own zero-valued SelfPair row.

Supply a native configuration to ask another routing question:

import netgraph_core as ngc

weighted = ngc.FlowPolicyConfig(routing=ngc.ShortestPaths(
    allocation=ngc.RouteAllocation.WEIGHTED,
    weight_basis=ngc.WeightBasis.CAPACITY,
))
query = CapacityQuery(Selector("^A$"), Selector("^C$"), config=weighted)
row = capacity(prepared, query).cases[0].states["converged"].rows[0]
assert row.result.delivered == 5

The normalized question records the effective model, finite offer/design inputs and failure request. How each model routes and admits traffic: Routing models and admission. offer and design_demand are optional physical inputs; the result names the question asked (MaxFlow). Native integer-valued configuration fields already contain units (Results and their units).

docs.title: Demands and placement
docs.text:
from ngraph import DemandSet, DemandSpec, PlacementQuery, place

traffic = DemandSet("traffic", (
    DemandSpec(Selector("^A$"), Selector("^C$"), volume=4),
))
loaded = prepare(Scenario(network, demand_sets={"traffic": traffic},
                          units=UnitsSettings(resolution=1)),
                 demand_sets=("traffic",))
placement = place(loaded, PlacementQuery(loaded.demand_sets["traffic"]))
assert placement.cases[0].states["converged"].totals.delivered_units == 4

DemandSpec accepts a declared preset, native configuration or named PinnedRoutes. Lower priorities are placed first; ties keep declaration order, then canonical expansion order. Ids are unique within a run; a demand without an id gets one from its set name and declaration index (Demand Fields). Splitting keeps each declared total: resolved plus discarded units equal declared units (Demands: how traffic enters).

With routing set to a RoutingDomain, wcmp_controller to a WCMPController (its scope) and forwarding_groups of ForwardingGroup values, each a router and its root ControllerGroups (ForwardingGroup(router, (ControllerGroup(children, share), ...)); children are GroupChild(share, edge=...) or nested GroupChild(share, children=...); shares are exact), every SHORTEST_PATHS_WCMP demand forwards on the controller's table toward its destination (Routing domains and the WCMP controller). ResolvedDemandSet.controller holds the tables (programmed routers and their member weights, and for all_routers each source's declared volume and weight). On such a set place accepts failure policies, and a dead group's cap is reported under dead_caps (Failures: patterns, cases and states). capacity refuses SHORTEST_PATHS_WCMP as its declaration.

docs.title: MSD
docs.text: maximum_supported_demand(prepared, MSDQuery(resolved_set)) searches for the largest tested feasible alpha (the demand-volume multiplier) of a resolved demand set (Maximum supported demand). alpha_feasible is the largest tested feasible alpha, or None when no probe was feasible; history holds every probe in order; search_status and stop_reason say how and why the search ended. export_probe_rows=True also exports every probe's rows (Python only).

docs.title: Tunnel counts
docs.text:
from ngraph import DemandSet, DemandSpec, TunnelCountQuery, tunnel_counts

te = ngc.FlowPolicyConfig(routing=ngc.CentralizedTE(
    source_allocation=ngc.SourceAllocation.EQUAL,
    tunnel_count=ngc.TunnelCount(1),
))
tunnels = DemandSet("tunnels", (
    DemandSpec(Selector("^A$"), Selector("^C$"), volume=0, policy=te),
))
counted = prepare(Scenario(network, demand_sets={"tunnels": tunnels},
                           units=UnitsSettings(resolution=1)),
                  demand_sets=("tunnels",))
counts = tunnel_counts(counted, TunnelCountQuery(
    counted.demand_sets["tunnels"], counts=(2, 4), design_demand=4, offer=6,
))
two, four = counts.rows
assert (two.count, two.result.plan.tunnels_per_head, two.result.delivered) == (2, 2, 5)
assert two.lossless_at_design_units == 4

tunnel_counts(prepared, TunnelCountQuery(demands, counts, design_demand, offer, up_to=None, eligibility=None, ...)) evaluates each tunnelled centralized-TE demand once per count (and once up to up_to), each a fresh native evaluation lossy at offer and planned for design_demand, the same two amounts for every demand. Each TunnelCountRow holds the native result (its plan is the tunnel layout), the row's count and up_to, lossless_at_design_units (min(design, the plan's largest lossless offer)) and physical_tunnel_cost (a pool row's tunnel cost without its one cost-1 ingress hop per tunnel). An eligibility (the engine's mask of usable nodes and edges, as FailureCase.eligibility holds) asks the question on a failed network. An offer above a TE ingress pool's prepared budget is refused: declare a TunnelCountAnalysis step with that offer and prepare again (Tunnels and TE ingress pools).

docs.title: Failure cases
docs.text:
from ngraph import FailureMode, FailurePolicy, FailureRequest, FailureRule

policy = FailurePolicy(modes=[FailureMode(1, [
    FailureRule("link", mode="choice", count=1),
])])
degraded = capacity(prepared, CapacityQuery(
    Selector("^A$"), Selector("^C$"),
    failures=FailureRequest(policy, iterations=20, seed=42),
    workers=2,
))
assert sum(case.case.occurrences for case in degraded.cases) == 20

failure_cases(prepared, request) exposes the same typed cases to custom analyses (Failures: patterns, cases and states; seeds: Seeds). For capacity, placement and sensitivity, workers="auto" resolves to the CPU count; results and errors are the same for any number of workers. MSD runs serially. Explicit worker values must be positive integers.

docs.title: Paths and sensitivity
docs.text:
paths(prepared, PathQuery(source, target)) returns one row in combine mode and one per selected source-group/destination-group pair in pairwise mode, holding the engine's Path values. SPF uses forward search; selectors supply the endpoints, so SpfOptions.targets must be None. In combine mode SPF keeps the paths of every source-destination node pair whose cost is the smallest of all pairs. costs_only=True returns costs without paths. A row with no route has cost=None; a node paired with itself has a self row of cost 0.

For K shortest paths, pass options=ngc.KspOptions(k, cost_ceiling=...). In combine mode the engine finds up to k paths for each source-destination node pair, and the row keeps the k cheapest of them all; equal costs keep node-pair order (sources, then destinations, by name), then the engine's order within a pair. An AbsoluteCost ceiling is inclusive; a CostStretch takes an exact fraction. An eligibility mask belongs to the prepared graph and has one flag per node and per edge; a residual vector has one integer per edge. The question records SPF's min_residual; KSP records None.

edge_sensitivity(prepared, SensitivityQuery(source, target, config, ...)) reports how much delivery falls without each directed link the engine tests: the engine's baseline result and one signed reduction per tested link (negative when removing the link helps). Python keeps the zero reductions; JSON leaves them out. It takes an uncapped lossless question or a finite lossy offer, and every reduction is measured against the baseline the result reports.

docs.title: Results and export
docs.text:
run(prepare(scenario)) returns RunResult with an ordered tuple of steps, the preparation's units report and producer metadata. Every analysis records its own typed query (CapacityQuery, PlacementQuery, SensitivityQuery, PathQuery, MSDQuery) as query, and a step records it as its question; a built-in domain step records itself. The JSON export writes each question in normalized form (selectors, the effective native model, failures, alpha and its source). A capacity case has states={"converged": ...}; a placement case has one entry per requested failure state (PlacementQuery.states, default ("converged",), "stale" and "repair" on request), and PlacementQuery.interaction selects "ordered" or "simultaneous" forwarding (workflow reference: TrafficMatrixPlacement). Each row holds the engine's result, with its endpoints, its reference request and any requested reports.

write_json(result, file) is the export path. It writes each plain record as its declared constants and fields, in declaration order; ngraph/schemas/results.json is generated from the same declarations. The file's format is in Output Format, and what its numbers mean in Results and their units.

CapacityQuery, PlacementQuery, SensitivityQuery, TunnelCountQuery and MSDQuery take export_details (default False), which adds the detail fields to the JSON only: row.result and the sensitivity baseline are always complete in Python. The analysis records it as outputs.details. MSD applies it to its best rows and any exported probe rows; its history stays compact.

docs.title: Custom steps and exporters
docs.text: A custom step implements run(context) -> StepOutput: it receives a StepContext, reads earlier successful steps through context.prior_results, and returns a StepOutput holding its question (a finite JSON mapping of its parameters) and its result. A step that needs a demand set bound, or asks a numerical question, says so with needs(), which returns a StepNeeds record (ngraph.workflow); the default None asks preparation for nothing. A custom result registers exactly one register_result_exporter(Type, encoder); plain JSON domain data is also accepted. Unknown result types refuse. The encoder runs once per requested export. Published results are immutable for later steps: plain JSON results and questions are stored read-only, and NetGraph's own records are immutable. A registered result is published as it is, with any native Core values it holds, so make its type immutable. A custom step type parses its own YAML keys by overriding the yaml_arguments(arguments, name) class method.

docs.title: Records and editing
docs.text:
Domain records are immutable from construction: nodes, links, risk groups, components, conditions, selectors, failure rules, modes and policies, demand declarations and built-in workflow steps. Each constructor checks its fields when the record is built, by one rule per kind of field, the same for Python and YAML: text is a str (a name is nonempty; whitespace is part of it), a flag a bool, an integer an int or an exactly integral float such as 2.0 (stored as 2), and an amount or ratio any finite real number in the field's range (stored as a float); a NumPy scalar of the field's kind counts as that kind, a subclass of str, int or float is stored as its plain value, and booleans are never numbers. Each refusal names the field and the value. What only the whole network can check (names that must exist, sums over links) is checked at preparation. attrs and condition operands must be finite JSON data and are stored read-only; tuples and sets in them are refused, so use lists. Record collections are stored as tuples and frozensets. Edit through the Network methods (add_node, add_link, replace_node, replace_link, the enable/disable and risk-group toggles) or dataclasses.replace: assigning a record field raises dataclasses.FrozenInstanceError, and editing read-only attrs raises TypeError. Network.add_link assigns a link's id once; a link already in a network is refused by another, so add dataclasses.replace(link) there. replace_link keeps a link's endpoints; to move a link, add a new one. A YAML declaration's identity is declared data that dataclasses.replace keeps: DemandSpec.yaml_label, declaration_ordinal and expand_leaf_index, and a step's yaml_label and derived_seed (its seed_source is scenario-derived while its seed equals that derived seed).

Network and ComponentsLibrary keep editable dicts. prepare changes nothing in its input: the returned PreparedScenario holds read-only views of those dicts, each copied on its own under plain string keys, that share the immutable records, so later edits of the caller's collections never reach it, and editing a prepared view raises TypeError. A failed prepare leaves its input as it was.

A custom step's own data is its own: it is neither copied nor frozen, and the step can change it and its later answers. prepare records each step's name and seed, so a later edit of those does not reach the prepared scenario. copy.copy, copy.deepcopy and pickle of a record give an equal immutable value; records that hold native values are shared by copies, and native values cannot be pickled.

docs.title: Domain tools and logging
docs.text:
BuildGraph exports the physical network in NetworkX node-link form. NetworkStats, CostPower and NetworkExplorer describe the network itself: its statistics, and its hardware cost and power. The risk-group methods of Network act on the group's members at the time of each call.

ngraph.hardware exports hardware_inventory, HardwareInventory, HardwareUse, link_active and resolve_link_end. ngraph.workflow.step_name(step) returns a step's effective run name. The public API is the __all__ of ngraph, ngraph.workflow, ngraph.hardware and ngraph.logging.

Importing the package installs a NullHandler. Applications can call ngraph.logging.set_global_log_level(level) or configure their own handler. Import the CLI explicitly when it is needed.

docs.title: Command Line
docs.text: The ngraph command inspects and runs scenarios from the terminal.

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
Two commands:

  • inspect: Load and validate a scenario and print its structure without running the workflow
  • run: Run the workflow and write results

Global options (must be placed before the command):

  • --verbose, -v: Enable debug logging
  • --quiet: Show only warnings and errors in logs (command output is still printed)

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
# Inspect a provided scenario
ngraph inspect scenarios/square_mesh.yaml

# Run a scenario (creates square_mesh.results.json by default)
ngraph run scenarios/square_mesh.yaml

docs.title: inspect
docs.text:
Load and validate a scenario and print its structure without running the workflow.

Syntax:

ngraph [--verbose|--quiet] inspect <scenario_file> [options]

Arguments:

  • scenario_file: Path to the YAML scenario file to inspect

Options:

  • --detail, -d: Show detailed information including complete node/link tables and step parameters

Output:

After loading and validating the scenario file, inspect reports:

  • Scenario metadata: seed, and whether the run is reproducible
  • Network structure: node/link counts, enabled vs. disabled, hierarchy
  • Capacity statistics: link and node capacity min/max/mean/median/total
  • Risk groups: defined groups, each enabled or disabled
  • Components library: components available to the scenario
  • Failure policies: each policy's mode count (modes and rules in detail mode)
  • Demand sets: demand patterns and volumes, capacity-vs-demand summary
  • Workflow steps: the steps that would run, in order, with their parameters in detail mode

A link counts as enabled when it and both of its end nodes are enabled, in every figure (Links, directions and what is enabled). The hierarchy groups nodes by the /-separated parts of their names, one level per part, and its counts include disabled nodes and links: a level's Links counts the links with an end inside it. With --detail, IntLinkCap sums the capacities of the links with both ends inside the level and ExtLinkCap of those with one end inside it, each link once. A selector preview reads <label>: G groups, N nodes (E enabled): the label is the selector's path (* without one) followed by its other parts, for example ^A [match: role == edge or tier == 1], * [group_by: role] or ^A [active_only: false]; N counts every node the selector matches with its active_only filter lifted, E the enabled ones among them, and G the groups of those N nodes. Each distinct selector is listed on its own, also when two share a path. A selection error during preview (for example a group key too large to write as text) prints ERROR with the reason, and invalid hardware prints under the hierarchy as Unable to analyze (...); inspect still finishes. An invalid demand or workflow selector pattern is refused at load, names the field and value, and makes inspect exit 1.

Examples:

# Basic inspection
ngraph inspect scenarios/backbone_clos.yml

# Detailed inspection with complete node/link tables and step parameters
ngraph inspect scenarios/nsfnet.yaml --detail

# Inspect with verbose logging (note: global option placement)
ngraph --verbose inspect scenarios/square_mesh.yaml

docs.title: run
docs.text:
Run the workflow of a scenario file and write the results.

Syntax:

ngraph [--verbose|--quiet] run <scenario_file> [options]

Arguments:

  • scenario_file: Path to the YAML scenario file to execute

Options:

  • --results, -r: Path to export results as JSON (default: <scenario_name>.results.json; relative paths are placed under --output when provided)
  • --no-results: Disable results file generation
  • --stdout: Print results to stdout in addition to saving file. Log output, status banners, the --profile performance report, and run error messages all go to stderr, so stdout contains only the JSON results (safe to pipe to jq)
  • --keys, -k: Space-separated list of workflow step names to include in output; an unknown name is an error
  • --profile: Print per-step wall time, process CPU time and the Python call profile to stderr
  • --profile-memory: Also track peak memory per step (requires --profile)
  • --output, -o: Output directory for the results file

docs.title: Basic Execution
docs.text:
# Default output file (square_mesh.results.json)
ngraph run scenarios/square_mesh.yaml

# Custom results path
ngraph run scenarios/backbone_clos.yml --results analysis.json

# Save and also print JSON to stdout
ngraph run scenarios/backbone_clos.yml --results analysis.json --stdout

# Run without writing any files
ngraph run scenarios/nsfnet.yaml --no-results

docs.title: Filtering Results by Step Names
docs.text:
--keys selects entries from the ordered steps array after the complete workflow executes. It keeps declaration order and each step's own execution_order, so a filtered export may have gaps. Unknown step names abort before any step executes:

# Only include results from the MSD step
ngraph run scenarios/square_mesh.yaml --keys msd_baseline --stdout

# Include multiple specific steps and save to custom file
ngraph run scenarios/backbone_clos.yml --keys network_statistics tm_placement --results filtered.json

# Filter and print to stdout while using default file
ngraph run scenarios/backbone_clos.yml --keys network_statistics --stdout

The names are the name fields of the steps in the scenario's workflow section.

docs.title: Performance Profiling
docs.text:
--profile reports where the run spends its time:

# Run scenario with profiling
ngraph run scenarios/backbone_clos.yml --profile

# Combine profiling with results export
ngraph run scenarios/backbone_clos.yml --profile --results analysis.json

# Track memory too, and export only the tm_placement step's results
ngraph run scenarios/backbone_clos.yml --profile --profile-memory --keys tm_placement

The report lists total elapsed time, time per step, steps taking more than 10% of the total and the Python call profile within those steps. A step's CPU time is the process's CPU time while it runs, across all threads and native work included, so CPU efficiency (CPU time over wall time) can exceed 100% when worker threads run. The function table ranks cProfile's internal time on the profiled thread; work on other threads appears only in the CPU totals, and work inside native routines is not split by C++ function. The report is printed to stderr.

docs.title: Output Format
docs.text:
The top-level fields are metadata, units_report and ordered steps. Each step contains its name, type, order, seed provenance, normalized question and typed result. For example, list the steps' questions and the bandwidth unit q with:

jq '{q: .units_report.q, steps: [.steps[] | {name, execution_order, question}]}' square_mesh.results.json

Each step's result is described with the step in Workflow Steps, and every field in Results. Native bandwidth amounts are integer units of the run's q, which the units report records; Results and their units lists the other kinds of numbers. Optional costs, cuts and edge arrays appear only when requested and applicable.

The results file and --stdout carry the same compact JSON: one line with no indentation or spaces after separators, non-ASCII characters kept, then a newline (jq . prints it indented). NaN is refused. Encoding completes before a results file is atomically replaced.

docs.title: Output Behavior
docs.text:
Command Writes Prints JSON ngraph run scenario.yaml <scenario_name>.results.json no ngraph run scenario.yaml --results out.json out.json no ngraph run scenario.yaml --stdout <scenario_name>.results.json yes ngraph run scenario.yaml --results out.json --stdout out.json yes ngraph run scenario.yaml --no-results nothing no ngraph run scenario.yaml --no-results --stdout nothing yes

run writes logs and status messages to stderr in every case. Exit status is 0 on success, 1 when the scenario cannot be loaded or run, and 2 for invalid command-line arguments.

docs.title: Debugging Scenarios
docs.text:
Inspect a scenario before running it. When blueprint expansion does not produce the nodes or links you expect, add --verbose and --detail:

ngraph inspect scenarios/square_mesh.yaml
ngraph --verbose inspect scenarios/backbone_clos.yml --detail
ngraph inspect scenarios/backbone_clos.yml --detail | grep -A 5 "WORKFLOW STEPS"

inspect reports YAML and schema errors, unknown blueprint or risk-group references and invalid workflow step parameters, and its node and demand tables show whether selectors matched what you expected.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: NetGraph is two layers. This page says what each does, what crosses between them, and what holds across them; How NetGraph computes explains the rules.

docs.title: Two layers
docs.text: NetGraph handles what the network means: physical topology, selectors, grouped demands, risk groups, scenarios and workflow questions. NetGraph-Core computes: graph searches, allocation, forwarding, tunnel holds and numerical results. A query names the engine model to run.

docs.title: The pipeline
docs.text:
• Prepare: NetGraph resolves selectors and demands on a read-only view of the editable network, chooses the bandwidth unit q and builds one immutable native graph.
  • Run: numerical analysis steps ask the Core their questions on the prepared graph. BuildGraph, NetworkStats and CostPower read the prepared domain records; custom steps run their own code. Numerical results hold the engine's result objects, which the export writes out.
  • Export: write_json writes the native results and NetGraph's records as JSON.

docs.title: Guarantees
docs.text:
• A call that fails publishes nothing: no partial analysis and no partial run.
  • Returned results stay readable after the scenario, its network and the prepared scenario are deleted.
  • Independent cases can run on worker threads. Drawing and output order do not depend on worker completion, and results are the same for any number of workers.

docs.title: Scenario YAML
docs.text: A scenario is a YAML file describing the network topology (nodes, links, risk groups), the analysis configuration (traffic demands, failure policies, workflow) and reusable parts (blueprints, hardware components). Every structure can be written out directly or generated from templates and parameters.

docs.title: Units and input validation
docs.text:
units:
  resolution: auto
  precision: 0.001
Key Default Meaning resolution auto The bandwidth unit q: auto, or one power of two from 2^-32 through 2^32 precision 0.001 The relative precision target, greater than 0 and at most 0.5, from which preparation chooses q; the units report states the input/count budget and whether its bounds hold

Capacities, demand volumes, finite offers and designs and minimum unreserved bandwidth are physical amounts, converted to whole units of q at preparation (Units and the resolution q); Precision and the choice of q says how q is chosen and what the units report records. Costs are positive integers (link keys); counts and weights are integers.

YAML reads a number written with an exponent only when it has a decimal point and a signed exponent: 1.0e+6 and 1.0e-12 are numbers, while 1e6, 1.0e6 and 1E+6 are text, and a numeric field refuses them:

network:
  nodes: {A: {}, B: {}}
  links: [{source: A, target: B, capacity: 1e6}]

Unknown keys are refused; your own metadata belongs under attrs. Every load refusal is a ValueError naming its field and raw value; a schema error is retained as the cause. An optional field accepts explicit null wherever its Python constructor accepts None.

docs.title: Template Syntaxes
docs.text:
Three template syntaxes, each valid only in its own context:

Syntax Example Where Effect [1-3] dc[1-3]/rack[a,b] Node and risk group names One definition per expansion, created at parse time $var / ${var} pod${p}/leaf Links, rules, demands Substituted from the vars of an expand block {n} srv-{n} template field 1-indexed counter up to count

docs.title: Selecting nodes
docs.text:
The DSL has two ways of selecting entities. Which one applies is fixed by the operation, not chosen by the author.

1. Path-Based Node Selection (link rules, traffic demands, workflow steps)

  • Regex patterns on hierarchical node names; capture groups define the groups
  • group_by regroups the selection by an attribute
  • match filters by attribute conditions
  • active_only drops disabled nodes

2. Condition-Based Entity Selection (failure rules, membership rules, risk group generation)

  • scope picks nodes, links or risk groups
  • conditions filter by attribute
  • An optional path regex filters by name (before conditions for membership and generate rules, after them for failure rules)

Both build on the same primitives (condition evaluation, match specification), but they are not interchangeable.

docs.title: Selector forms
docs.text:
Selectors can be specified as:

  1. String pattern: A regular expression matched against node names from the start (Python re.match)
  2. Selector object: A dict with path, group_by, and/or match fields

At least one of path, group_by, or match must be specified in a selector object.

docs.title: String patterns
docs.text:
# Exact match
- source: "spine-1"

# Prefix match
- source: "dc1/spine/"

# Wildcard patterns
- source: "dc1/leaf.*"

# Anchored patterns
- source: "^dc1/spine/switch-[1-3]$"

# Alternation
- source: "^dc1/(spine|leaf)/.*$"

docs.title: Capturing groups
docs.text:
Regex capturing groups create node groupings for analysis:

# Single group: (dc\d+)
# Creates groups: "dc1", "dc2", etc.

# Multiple groups: (dc\d+)/(spine|leaf)/switch-(\d+)
# Creates groups: "dc1|spine|1", "dc1|leaf|2", etc.

Group Behavior:

  • Single capturing group: Group by captured value
  • Multiple capturing groups: Join with | separator
  • No capturing groups: one group of every matched node, labelled by the pattern string

docs.title: Attribute-based grouping
docs.text:
Use the group_by field to group nodes by an attribute value:

# Group by metro attribute
- source:
    group_by: "metro"

# Combine with path filtering
- source:
    path: "^dc1/.*"
    group_by: "role"

Notes:

  • group_by refers to a top-level field (name, disabled, risk_groups) or a key in node.attrs. Nested (dot-notation) keys are not supported.
  • Nodes without the specified attribute are omitted.
  • Group labels are the string form of the attribute value.

docs.title: Attribute-based filtering
docs.text:
Use the match field to filter nodes by attribute conditions:

source:
  path: "^dc1/.*"
  match:
    logic: "and"           # "and" or "or" (default: "or")
    conditions:
      - attr: "role"
        op: "=="
        value: "leaf"
      - attr: "tier"
        op: ">="
        value: 2

See Conditions for the operators and the condition syntax.

docs.title: Conditions
docs.text:
Every selection mechanism evaluates conditions the same way.

1. Condition Structure

Each condition has three fields:

conditions:
  - attr: "role"           # Attribute name (supports dot-notation)
    op: "=="               # Operator
    value: "leaf"          # Expected value

2. Condition Operators

Operator Description Example == Equals {attr: "role", op: "==", value: "leaf"} != Not equals {attr: "tier", op: "!=", value: 1} < Less than (numeric) {attr: "cost", op: "<", value: 100} <= Less than or equal {attr: "priority", op: "<=", value: 5} > Greater than (numeric) {attr: "capacity", op: ">", value: 1000} >= Greater than or equal {attr: "tier", op: ">=", value: 2} contains String contains or collection includes {attr: "name", op: "contains", value: "spine"} not_contains String/collection does not include {attr: "tags", op: "not_contains", value: "deprecated"} in Value is in provided list {attr: "role", op: "in", value: ["leaf", "spine"]} not_in Value is not in provided list {attr: "dc", op: "not_in", value: ["dc3", "dc4"]} exists Attribute exists and is not null {attr: "hardware.vendor", op: "exists"} not_exists Attribute missing or null {attr: "deprecated", op: "not_exists"}

Operator semantics:

  • Ordering operators (<, <=, >, >=) compare integer and finite float operands exactly, including integers too large for a float. Other operands are coerced to float when possible, so "10" > 5 is true; equality (==, !=) does not coerce, so "10" == 10 is false. Keep attribute and condition value types consistent.
  • For a missing or null attribute, every operator except not_exists returns false, including the negative ones (!=, not_contains, not_in). Use not_exists to match absent attributes.
  • in/not_in require a list value; a scalar is refused where the condition is given (YAML at load, Python when the Condition is built).

3. Condition Combining (logic)

  • "or" (default in most contexts): Any condition must match
  • "and": All conditions must match
match:
  logic: "and"
  conditions:
    - {attr: "role", op: "==", value: "leaf"}
    - {attr: "tier", op: ">=", value: 2}

4. Attribute Access

Conditions evaluate against a flattened view of entity attributes: - Node top-level fields: name, disabled, risk_groups - Link top-level fields: id, source, target, capacity, cost, disabled, risk_groups - Risk group top-level fields (rules with scope: risk_group): name, disabled, children (list of child group names) - Custom attributes from attrs block (top-level fields take precedence on key conflicts)

5. Dot-Notation for Nested Attributes

Access nested attributes using dots:

conditions:
  - attr: "hardware.vendor"      # Resolves to attrs["hardware"]["vendor"]
    op: "=="
    value: "Acme"

6. Variable Expansion

Template expansion ($var, ${var}) is processed before condition evaluation (see Variable Expansion).

docs.title: Active-only filtering and context defaults
docs.text:
Use active_only to control whether disabled nodes are included:

# Override default to include disabled nodes in demands
- source:
    path: "^dc1/.*"
    active_only: false    # Include disabled nodes (overrides demand default of true)

# Override default to exclude disabled nodes in links
- source:
    path: "^dc1/.*"
    active_only: true     # Exclude disabled nodes (overrides link default of false)

Defaults differ by context and can be set explicitly per selector:

Context Selection active_only default match.logic default Links Path-based false (links to disabled nodes are created) "or" Demands Path-based true (only active nodes take traffic) "or" Node rules Path-based false "or" Workflow steps Path-based true (only the active topology is analyzed) "or" Membership rules Condition-based N/A "and" Failure rules Condition-based N/A "or" Generate blocks Condition-based N/A N/A (no conditions; groups by values)

Path-based selection supports capture groups, group_by, match and variable expansion, over nodes only. Condition-based selection scans nodes, links or risk groups with an optional path regex and no capture groups or variable expansion; match applies to membership and failure rules, and group_by to generate blocks.

docs.title: Links
docs.text:
A link definition is processed in five steps:

  1. Path Selection: Regex pattern matches nodes by hierarchical name - Capture groups create initial grouping - If no path specified, selects all nodes
  2. Attribute Filtering: Optional match conditions filter nodes - Uses logic: "and" or "or" (default: "or") - Operators are listed under Conditions
  3. Active Filtering: Filters disabled nodes based on context - Links default: active_only=false (creates links to disabled nodes)
  4. Attribute Grouping: Optional group_by overrides regex capture grouping
  5. Pattern Application: Creates links between selected node groups - mesh: Every source to every target - one_to_one: Pairwise with wrap-around

docs.title: Demands
docs.text:
Traffic demands select nodes the same way as links, with these differences:

  1. active_only defaults to true: only active nodes participate
  2. Two selections, source nodes first and then target nodes, each with path, match and group_by
  3. mode and group_mode decide how the selections produce demands (Traffic Modes, Group Modes)

docs.title: Risk groups
docs.text:
Risk groups use the condition-based model and are populated in three ways:

  1. Direct definition: the group is named and entities reference it
  2. Membership rules: entities whose attributes match are assigned to the group
  3. Generate blocks: one group per distinct value of an attribute

Membership rules and generate blocks scan every entity of their scope; an optional path regex narrows candidates by name (links match against their source|target form), conditions filter by attribute, and membership logic defaults to and.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
A workflow step's selectors:

workflow:
  - type: MaxFlow
    source:
      group_by: "metro"      # Group by metro attribute
    target: "^metro2/.*"     # String pattern
    mode: "pairwise"

A link definition's selectors:

network:
  nodes:
    dc1:
      nodes:
        spine: {count: 2, attrs: {role: spine}}
    dc2:
      nodes:
        leaf: {count: 2, attrs: {role: leaf}}
  links:
    - source:
        group_by: "role"
      target:
        path: "^dc2/leaf/.*"
      pattern: mesh

docs.title: Top-Level Keys
docs.text:
network: {}              # Network topology
blueprints: {}           # Reusable network templates
components: {}           # Hardware component library
risk_groups: []          # Failure correlation groups
vars: {}                 # YAML anchors and variables for reuse
demands: {}              # Traffic demand definitions
failures: {}             # Failure simulation policies
workflow: []             # Analysis execution steps
seed: 42                 # Scenario seed for reproducibility (integer)
units: {resolution: auto, precision: 0.001}  # Bandwidth unit q and precision target
routes: {}               # Named explicit routes
supports: {}             # Named forwarding supports (DAGs)
weights: {}              # Named edge weights
routing:                 # IGP domain and BGP-edge routers for the WCMP controller
  igp_domain: {path: "^core"}
  bgp_edge: {path: "^edge"}
wcmp_controller: {scope: next_hop}  # WCMP controller scope
forwarding_groups: {}    # Fixed group shares at programmed routers
Key Required Description network No Network topology: nodes, links, and rules blueprints No Reusable topology templates components No Hardware component library for cost/power modeling risk_groups No Failure correlation groups for resilience analysis vars No YAML anchors for reuse within the scenario demands No Traffic demand patterns for capacity analysis failures No Failure policies for simulation workflow No Analysis workflow steps to execute seed No Scenario seed (integer) for reproducible random operations units No Bandwidth unit q (resolution, auto by default) and precision target (Units) routes No Named explicit routes for pinned models supports No Named forwarding supports (DAGs of directed links) weights No Named edge-weight tables routing With wcmp_controller IGP domain and BGP-edge populations (WCMP controller) wcmp_controller No Controller scope for SHORTEST_PATHS_WCMP demands forwarding_groups No Declared group trees at routers the controller programs (needs wcmp_controller)

All sections are optional. A scenario that omits network entirely, or sets it to an empty mapping (network: {}), builds with an empty topology. A bare network: with no value is a YAML null and fails schema validation. Any unrecognized top-level key is rejected during JSON Schema validation with a ValueError whose cause is the schema's ValidationError (the schema sets additionalProperties: false).

docs.title: Seeds
docs.text: A workflow step's failure draws use the step's seed: its own seed, or one derived from the scenario seed: the SHA-256 of the UTF-8 string <seed>:workflow_step:<step-name>, its first four bytes read as a big-endian integer and masked with 0x7fffffff. A library FailureRequest that names a scenario policy and gives no seed of its own uses the policy's seed, derived the same way from <seed>:failure_policy:failure_policy:<name>: scenario seed 42 and policy random_link yield 2099469712. Failure draw i creates random.Random(base_seed + i); without a base seed every draw is unseeded and results vary between runs. A random rule fails each matched entity independently with its probability: one random number per entity, in sorted identifier order, the same on every supported Python. Results record the seed, where it came from, the runtime, the generator and the draw order.

docs.title: network - Topology
docs.text:
Nodes and links, written out directly or generated from node groups and link definitions.

Network metadata fields:

network:
  name: "my-network"       # Optional network name (stored in network.attrs)
  version: "1.0"           # Optional version (stored in network.attrs)
  nodes: {}                # Node definitions (see below)
  links: []                # Link definitions (see below)

docs.title: Direct Node and Link Definitions
docs.text:
Individual Nodes:

network:
  nodes:
    SEA:
      disabled: true
      attrs:
        coords: [47.6062, -122.3321]
        hardware:
          component: "LeafRouter"
          count: 1
    SFO:
      attrs:
        coords: [37.7749, -122.4194]
        hardware:
          component: "SpineRouter"
          count: 1

Recognized keys for each node entry:

  • disabled: boolean (optional)
  • attrs: mapping of attributes (optional)
  • risk_groups: list of risk-group names (optional)

Individual Links:

network:
  nodes: {SEA: {}, SFO: {}}
  links:
    - source: SEA
      target: SFO
      capacity: 200
      cost: 6846
      attrs:
        distance_km: 1369.13
        media_type: "fiber"
        hardware:
          source: {component: "800G-ZR+", count: 1}
          target: {component: "1600G-2xDR4", count: 1}

Recognized keys for each link entry:

  • source, target: node names (required)
  • capacity: link capacity (optional; default 1.0)
  • cost: link cost (optional; default 1), an integer from 1 to below 2^62; an exactly integral value such as 1.0 is stored as 1, and any other value is refused where it is given
  • disabled: boolean (optional)
  • risk_groups: list of risk-group names (optional)
  • attrs: mapping of attributes (optional)
  • count: integer number of parallel links to create (optional; default 1); loading takes time linear in it

A link entry whose source or target matches no node is refused at load, naming its position and endpoints. Node and link rules that match nothing remain silent. Each physical link carries traffic in both directions (Links, directions and what is enabled).

docs.title: Node Groups
docs.text:
Node Groups with Count/Template:

network:
  nodes:
    leaf:
      count: 4
      template: "leaf-{n}"
      attrs:
        role: "leaf"
    spine:
      count: 2
      template: "spine-{n}"
      attrs:
        role: "spine"

Creates: leaf/leaf-1, leaf/leaf-2, leaf/leaf-3, leaf/leaf-4, spine/spine-1, spine/spine-2

Loading a node group takes work linear in its count. The {n} placeholder is replaced with a 1-indexed counter (1, 2, 3, ...) up to count. The group name becomes the parent path, and template generates child node names. When count is given without template, the template defaults to <group>-{n} (so leaf: {count: 2} creates leaf/leaf-1 and leaf/leaf-2).

Nested Nodes (Inline Hierarchy):

Create hierarchical node structures without blueprints using nested nodes:

network:
  nodes:
    dc1:
      nodes:                    # Inline nested hierarchy
        rack1:
          count: 4
          template: "srv-{n}"
          attrs:
            role: "server"
        rack2:
          count: 4
          template: "srv-{n}"
          attrs:
            role: "server"
        tor:
          count: 2
          template: "tor-{n}"
          attrs:
            role: "switch"

Creates: dc1/rack1/srv-1, dc1/rack1/srv-2, ..., dc1/tor/tor-1, dc1/tor/tor-2

Use nested nodes for one-off hierarchies. For structures repeated across the scenario, use blueprints.

Link Definitions:

network:
  nodes:
    leaf: {count: 4}
    spine: {count: 2}
  links:
    - source: /leaf
      target: /spine
      pattern: "mesh"           # Connect every leaf to every spine
      capacity: 3200
      cost: 1
    - source: /spine
      target: /spine
      pattern: "mesh"           # Connect every spine to every other spine
      count: 2                   # Create 2 parallel links per pair (optional)
      capacity: 1600
      cost: 1
      attrs:
        hardware:
          source: {component: "800G-DR4", count: 2}
          target: {component: "800G-DR4", count: 2}

docs.title: Attribute-filtered Links (selector objects)
docs.text:
To filter the source or target node sets by attributes, replace a string source/target with an object that has path and optional match. The condition syntax is the same as in failure policies:

network:
  nodes:
    leaf: {count: 2, attrs: {role: leaf}}
    spine: {count: 2, attrs: {role: spine}}
  links:
    - source:
        path: "/leaf"
        match:
          logic: "and"         # default: "or"
          conditions:
            - attr: "role"
              op: "=="
              value: "leaf"
      target:
        path: "/spine"
        match:
          conditions:
            - attr: "role"
              op: "=="
              value: "spine"
      pattern: "mesh"
      capacity: 100
      cost: 1

Notes:

  • path is a regex pattern matched against node names (anchored at start via Python re.match).
  • match.conditions uses the shared condition operators: ==, !=, <, <=, >, >=, contains, not_contains, in, not_in, exists, not_exists.
  • Conditions evaluate over a flat view of node attributes combining top-level fields (name, disabled, risk_groups) and node.attrs.
  • logic in the match block accepts "and" or "or" (default "or").
  • Selectors filter node candidates before the link pattern is applied.
  • Cross-endpoint predicates (e.g., comparing a source attribute to a target attribute) are not supported.
  • Node rules run before link expansion; link rules run after link creation.

Path semantics:

  • All paths are relative to the current scope. There is no concept of absolute paths.
  • A leading / is stripped, so /leaf and leaf are equivalent.
  • Within a blueprint, paths resolve relative to the instantiation path. For example, if a blueprint is used under group pod1, then source: /leaf resolves to pod1/leaf.
  • At top-level network.links, the parent path is empty, so patterns match against full node names.

Example with OR logic to match multiple roles:

network:
  nodes:
    metro1:
      nodes:
        dc1: {attrs: {role: dc}}
        pop1: {attrs: {role: leaf}}
        pop2: {attrs: {role: core}}
  links:
    - source:
        path: "/metro1/dc[1-1]"
        match:
          conditions:
            - attr: "role"
              op: "=="
              value: "dc"
      target:
        path: "/metro1/pop[1-2]"
        match:
          logic: "or"
          conditions:
            - attr: "role"
              op: "=="
              value: "leaf"
            - attr: "role"
              op: "=="
              value: "core"
      pattern: "mesh"

Connectivity Patterns:

  • mesh: Full connectivity between all source and target nodes
  • one_to_one: Pairwise connections. Compatible sizes means max(|S|,|T|) must be an integer multiple of min(|S|,|T|); mapping wraps modulo the smaller set (e.g., 4x2 and 6x3 valid; 3x2 invalid). Self-pairs are skipped, so one_to_one between a group and itself creates no links; use mesh to interconnect a group with itself.

docs.title: Bracket Expansion
docs.text:
Create multiple similar node groups using bracket notation:

network:
  nodes:
    dc[1-3]/rack[a,b]:     # Creates dc1/racka, dc1/rackb, dc2/racka, etc.
      count: 4
      template: "srv-{n}"

Expansion Types:

  • Numeric ranges: [1-4] -> 1, 2, 3, 4
  • Explicit lists: [red,blue,green] -> red, blue, green
  • Mixed expressions: [1,3,5-7] -> 1, 3, 5, 6, 7
  • Multiple brackets: Cartesian product of all brackets
# Multiple brackets produce cartesian product
dc[1-2]/rack[a,b]: {}   # Creates: dc1/racka, dc1/rackb, dc2/racka, dc2/rackb

Scope: Bracket expansion applies to:

  • Node names under network.nodes and blueprints.*.nodes, including direct single-node entries without count/template (SEA[1-2]: {} creates nodes SEA1 and SEA2)
  • Risk group names in top-level risk_groups definitions (including children)
  • Risk group membership arrays on nodes, links, node groups, and in node/link rules

Component names and other string fields treat brackets as literal characters. (Link source/target strings are regexes, where [...] is a character class, not bracket expansion.)

Risk Group Expansion Examples:

# Definition expansion - creates DC1_Power, DC2_Power, DC3_Power
risk_groups:
  - name: "DC[1-3]_Power"
  - name: "RG[1-3]"        # Defines RG1, RG2, RG3 (referenced below)

# Membership expansion - assigns to RG1, RG2, RG3
network:
  nodes:
    Server:
      risk_groups: ["RG[1-3]"]

Limitations and Workarounds:

Pattern Behavior Workaround [01-03] Produces 1, 2, 3 (no leading zeros) Use explicit list: [01,02,03] [A-C] Error (letter ranges not supported) Use explicit list: [A,B,C] [1-10] Produces 1, 2, ..., 10 Works correctly

The range syntax [start-end] only supports integers. For letters, mixed sequences, or zero-padded numbers, use comma-separated explicit lists.

docs.title: Variable Expansion
docs.text:
Use $var or ${var} syntax with an expand block for template substitution. Variables are recursively substituted in all string fields within the block, including nested attrs.

Type preservation: A value consisting of exactly one placeholder (e.g. value: "${t}") is replaced by the variable's native value, preserving its type, so match conditions compare correctly against numeric node/link attributes. Placeholders embedded in longer strings (e.g. "dc${dc}_internal") interpolate as text and always produce strings. A bare placeholder bound to a non-string variable used where a path selector is required (e.g. source: "${n}" with n: [1, 2]) raises ValueError instead of being silently stringified; use an embedded form such as "dc${n}/leaf" for selector strings.

Supported contexts:

  • Link definitions (network.links and blueprints.*.links)
  • Link rules (network.link_rules)
  • Node rules (network.node_rules)
  • Traffic demands (demands.*)

Expansion modes:

Mode Behavior Example cartesian (default) All combinations of variable values p:[1,2], r:[a,b] → 4 expansions zip Pair values by index (lists must have equal length) a:[1,2], b:[x,y] → 2 expansions

Cartesian expansion and reversed pairs: Each variable combination of an expand block is an independent link definition. Reversed-pair deduplication applies only within one combination, so cartesian expansion over symmetric variable lists (e.g. vars: {a: [1, 2], b: [1, 2]} with source: "dc${a}/gw", target: "dc${b}/gw") creates both orientations as separate parallel links, doubling capacity. To mesh one node set, prefer a single mesh definition with a regex selector (e.g. source: "dc[0-9]+/gw", target: "dc[0-9]+/gw", pattern: mesh), which deduplicates reversed pairs.

Example in links:

links:
  - source: "plane${p}/rack${r}"
    target: "spine${s}"
    expand:
      vars:
        p: [1, 2]
        r: ["a", "b"]
        s: [1, 2, 3]
      mode: "cartesian"  # 2 × 2 × 3 = 12 link definitions
    pattern: "mesh"

  - source: "server${idx}"
    target: "switch${idx}"
    expand:
      vars:
        idx: [1, 2, 3, 4]
      mode: "zip"        # 4 paired link definitions
    pattern: "one_to_one"

Variables in nested attributes:

links:
  - source: "${dc}/leaf"
    target: "${dc}/spine"
    expand:
      vars:
        dc: ["dc1", "dc2"]
    attrs:
      datacenter: "${dc}"      # Also substituted
      corridor: "${dc}_internal"
    pattern: "mesh"

Limits: Expansion is capped at 10,000 items per block to prevent accidental combinatorial explosion.

docs.title: blueprints - Reusable Templates
docs.text:
Templates for network segments, instantiated as many times as needed:

blueprints:
  leaf_spine:
    nodes:
      leaf:
        count: 4
        template: "leaf-{n}"
      spine:
        count: 2
        template: "spine-{n}"
    links:
      - source: /leaf
        target: /spine
        pattern: mesh
        capacity: 40
        cost: 1

network:
  nodes:
    pod1:
      blueprint: leaf_spine
    pod2:
      blueprint: leaf_spine
      params:                    # Override blueprint parameters
        leaf.count: 6
        spine.template: "core-{n}"

Instance names are prefixed with the group name: pod1/leaf/leaf-1, pod2/spine/core-1.

Parameter override rules:

  • Override keys must be of the form <group>.<field>, where <group> is a literal (unexpanded) subgroup name defined in the blueprint. Unknown group prefixes or bare keys (no dot) raise ValueError at scenario build time.
  • Override keys are matched against literal blueprint subgroup names by the longest <group>. prefix (not by splitting on the first dot), so subgroup names containing dots (e.g. rack.a) are addressable as rack.a.count. When one subgroup name is a dotted extension of another (e.g. rack and rack.a), the longest matching name receives the override.
  • To override parameters of a nested blueprint, use a dict value under <group>.params:
blueprints:
  leaf_spine:
    nodes:
      leaf:
        count: 4
      spine:
        count: 2
  two_pod_dc:
    nodes:
      pod1:
        blueprint: leaf_spine
      pod2:
        blueprint: leaf_spine

network:
  nodes:
    dc1:
      blueprint: two_pod_dc
      params:
        pod1.params:             # Dict-valued pass-through to the nested blueprint
          spine.count: 8

The dotted form pod1.params.spine.count is rejected.

docs.title: Node and Link Rules
docs.text: Modify specific nodes or links after initial creation. Rules run post-expansion and can override properties, add attributes, or disable elements.

docs.title: Node Rules
docs.text:
network:
  node_rules:
    # Simple path-based matching
    - path: "^pod1/spine/.*$"
      disabled: true
      attrs:
        maintenance_mode: "active"

    # Path with attribute filtering
    - path: "^dc1/.*"
      match:
        logic: "and"
        conditions:
          - attr: "role"
            op: "=="
            value: "leaf"
          - attr: "tier"
            op: ">="
            value: 2
      attrs:
        priority: "high"

    # Variable expansion for repeated rules
    - path: "^${dc}/rack1/.*"
      expand:
        vars:
          dc: ["dc1", "dc2", "dc3"]
      attrs:
        zone: "${dc}_zone1"

Node rule fields:

  • path: Regex pattern matched against node names (optional; defaults to .*, matching all nodes)
  • match: Optional attribute conditions to filter matched nodes
  • disabled: Set node disabled state
  • attrs: Attributes to merge into matched nodes
  • risk_groups: Risk groups for matched nodes; replaces the node's existing risk_groups set (it does not add to it)
  • expand: Variable expansion block for templated rules

docs.title: Link Rules
docs.text:
network:
  link_rules:
    # Basic endpoint matching
    - source: "^pod1/leaf/.*$"
      target: "^pod1/spine/.*$"
      capacity: 100

    # Bidirectional matching (default: true)
    - source: ".*/spine/.*"
      target: ".*/spine/.*"
      bidirectional: true
      cost: 5
      attrs:
        link_type: "backbone"

    # Filter by link's own attributes using link_match
    - source: "^dc1/.*"
      target: "^dc2/.*"
      link_match:
        logic: "and"
        conditions:
          - attr: "link_type"
            op: "=="
            value: "inter_dc"
          - attr: "capacity"
            op: ">="
            value: 100
      cost: 10
      attrs:
        priority: "high"

    # Variable expansion
    - source: "^${src}/.*"
      target: "^${dst}/.*"
      expand:
        vars:
          src: ["dc1", "dc2"]
          dst: ["dc2", "dc3"]
        mode: "zip"
      attrs:
        corridor: "${src}_to_${dst}"

Link rule fields:

  • source, target: Regex patterns or selector objects for endpoint matching (both required on every rule)
  • bidirectional: Match links in both directions (default: true)
  • link_match: Filter by link's own attributes (not endpoint attributes)
  • capacity, cost, disabled: Override link properties, by the same rules as a link declaration
  • attrs: Attributes to merge into matched links
  • risk_groups: Risk groups for matched links; replaces the link's existing risk_groups set (it does not add to it)
  • expand: Variable expansion block for templated rules

Execution order:

  1. node_rules run after node creation but before link expansion
  2. link_rules run after all links are created

docs.title: components - Hardware Library
docs.text:
Define hardware components with attributes for cost and power modeling. A component’s count is a positive integer whose conversion to float is finite, checked when the component is declared:

components:
  SpineRouter:
    component_type: "chassis"
    description: "64-port spine router"
    capex: 50000.0
    power_watts: 2500.0
    power_watts_max: 3000.0
    capacity: 64000.0           # Gbps
    ports: 64
    attrs:
      vendor: "VendorName"
      model: "Model-9000"
    children:
      LineCard400G:
        component_type: "linecard"
        capex: 8000.0
        power_watts: 400.0
        capacity: 12800.0
        ports: 32
        count: 4

  Optic400G:
    component_type: "optic"
    description: "400G pluggable optic"
    capex: 2500.0
    power_watts: 12.0
    capacity: 400.0
    attrs:
      reach: "10km"
      wavelength: "1310nm"

Component Usage:

network:
  nodes:
    spine-1:
      attrs:
        hardware:
          component: "SpineRouter"
          count: 2   # Optional positive multiplier; defaults to 1
    leaf-1: {}
  links:
    - source: spine-1
      target: leaf-1
      attrs:
        hardware:
          source: {component: "Optic400G", count: 4}
          target: {component: "Optic400G", count: 4}

hardware, and each of a link's source and target, must be a mapping (null counts as absent). count (default 1) must be a finite positive number that fits a float, whether or not the node or link is enabled; the CostPower step and the network explorer refuse any other value with a ValueError naming the node or link end (for example link a|b|0 source end: ...), before any capacity or port check. A link end counts only where its endpoint node has hardware. A link end's exclusive must be a boolean: true marks its hardware as not shared with other links; the explorer's bill of materials then rounds that end's count up to a whole unit, while cost, power and ports use the declared count. Hardware totals too large for a finite float are refused with the entity and field named. Bill-of-materials counts are float sums: integer counts are exact while a total stays at most 2^53.

docs.title: risk_groups - Risk Modeling
docs.text:
Risk groups model correlated failures as hierarchies: physical infrastructure, geographic regions, vendor dependencies, or custom domains.

Identical repeated inline group declarations resolve once. Conflicting inline attributes, disabled flags, membership declarations or child declarations refuse with both parent paths. A registered top-level declaration takes precedence over inline references of the same name.

docs.title: Hierarchy
docs.text:
Risk groups form parent-child trees that model cascading failures:

risk_groups:
  - name: "Region_West"
    children:
      - name: "Site_Seattle"
      - name: "Site_Portland"

Cascading semantics: When a parent fails, all descendants fail with it: a regional outage takes every site in the region.

Storage model: Children are nested within parents, not in the top-level dictionary:

from ngraph import Scenario

scenario = Scenario.from_yaml("""
risk_groups:
  - {name: Region_West, children: [{name: Site_Seattle}, {name: Site_Portland}]}
""")
assert list(scenario.network.risk_groups) == ["Region_West"]
region = scenario.network.risk_groups["Region_West"]
assert [child.name for child in region.children] == ["Site_Seattle", "Site_Portland"]

String shorthand: an entry that is a bare string defines a group with that name and no other fields: - "Region_West" is equivalent to - name: "Region_West". The same shorthand works inside children.

Disabled groups: disabled: true on a top-level group disables every member node and link at scenario load, including members of its descendant groups. This runs after membership rules and generate blocks, so entities assigned by those mechanisms are covered.

Top-level-only keys: membership, disabled, and generate are honored only on top-level risk_groups entries. Nested children entries allow only name, attrs, and children; placing any other key on a child is rejected by the JSON schema at scenario load and by the parser with ValueError. Define such groups at top level and reference them by name as children.

Entity references: a node or link names the risk groups it belongs to. Any declared group can be named: a top-level group, or a child at any depth with no top-level entry of its own. A failed group fails its own members and the members of every group below it:

risk_groups:
  - name: Region_West
    children:
      - name: Site_Seattle
      - name: Site_Portland

network:
  nodes:
    Router_SEA: {risk_groups: [Site_Seattle]}
    Router_PDX: {risk_groups: [Site_Portland]}
    Router_SFO: {}
  links:
    - {source: Router_SEA, target: Router_PDX, capacity: 10}
    - {source: Router_PDX, target: Router_SFO, capacity: 10, risk_groups: [Region_West]}

Failing Site_Seattle fails Router_SEA; failing Region_West fails Router_SEA, Router_PDX and the link Router_PDX|Router_SFO|0.

docs.title: Example 1: Physical Infrastructure (Fiber Links)
docs.text:
For fiber links, a hierarchy of Path -> Conduit -> Fiber Pair mirrors the physical plant.

risk_groups:
  # Each conduit declared once, with its attributes
  - name: "Conduit_NYC_CHI_C[1-2]"
    attrs:
      type: fiber_conduit

  # The hierarchy names them as its children: its failure fails theirs
  - name: "Path_NYC_CHI"
    attrs:
      type: fiber_path
      distance_km: 1200
    children:
      - name: "Conduit_NYC_CHI_C[1-2]"

network:
  nodes:
    NYC: {}
    CHI: {}
  links:
    - source: NYC
      target: CHI
      risk_groups: ["Conduit_NYC_CHI_C1"]
      attrs:
        fiber:
          path_id: "NYC-CHI"
          conduit_id: "NYC-CHI-C1"

Cascading behavior:

  • Fiber pair failure affects only that pair
  • Conduit failure affects all pairs in that conduit
  • Path failure affects all conduits in that path

docs.title: Example 2: Physical Infrastructure (Data Center Nodes)
docs.text:
For data center nodes, a hierarchy of Building -> Room -> Power Zone mirrors the facility.

risk_groups:
  # Each power zone declared once, with its attributes
  - name: "PowerZone_DC1_R1_PZ[A,B]"
    attrs:
      type: power_zone

  # The hierarchy names them under the rooms: a room's or the building's failure
  # fails theirs
  - name: "Building_DC1"
    attrs:
      type: building
      location: "Ashburn, VA"
    children:
      - name: "Room_DC1_R[1-3]"
        attrs:
          type: room
        children:
          - name: "PowerZone_DC1_R1_PZ[A,B]"

network:
  nodes:
    Router_DC1_R1_RK01:
      risk_groups: ["PowerZone_DC1_R1_PZA"]
      attrs:
        facility:
          building_id: "DC1"
          room_id: "DC1-R1"
          power_zone: "DC1-R1-PZ-A"

Cascading behavior:

  • Power zone failure affects equipment in that zone
  • Room failure affects all zones in that room
  • Building failure affects entire site

docs.title: Example 3: Geographic/Administrative Grouping
docs.text:
For geographic or administrative modeling:

risk_groups:
  - name: "Region_West"
    attrs:
      type: geographic
    children:
      - name: "AZ_US_West_1a"
      - name: "AZ_US_West_1b"
  - name: "MaintenanceWindow_Weekend"
    attrs:
      type: operational
      schedule: "Sat-Sun 02:00-06:00 UTC"

docs.title: Membership Rules
docs.text:
Assign entities to a risk group by attribute:

risk_groups:
  - name: Conduit_NYC_CHI_C1
    membership:
      scope: link
      match:
        logic: and           # "and" or "or" (default: "and")
        conditions:
          - attr: fiber.conduit_id
            op: "=="
            value: "NYC-CHI-C1"

  - name: PowerZone_DC1_R1_PZA
    membership:
      scope: node
      match:
        logic: and
        conditions:
          - attr: facility.power_zone
            op: "=="
            value: "DC1-R1-PZ-A"

Membership rules default to logic: "and", stricter than link and demand selectors, which default to "or".

A membership rule requires scope plus at least one of path or match; a match block must contain at least one condition. The optional path regex pre-filters candidates by name before conditions are evaluated (links match against their source|target form).

docs.title: Generated Risk Groups
docs.text:
One risk group per distinct attribute value:

risk_groups:
  # Generate risk groups from fiber path attributes on links
  - generate:
      scope: link
      group_by: fiber.path_id
      name: Path_${value}
      attrs:
        type: fiber_path

  # Generate risk groups from facility attributes on nodes
  - generate:
      scope: node
      group_by: facility.building_id
      name: Building_${value}
      attrs:
        type: building

A generate block requires scope (node or link), group_by (supports dot-notation), and name; name must contain the ${value} placeholder. An optional path regex pre-filters entities by name (links match against their source|target form). Errors raised as ValueError: a group_by attribute resolving to an unhashable value (e.g. a list), a name template rendering the same group name for two distinct attribute values, and a generated name colliding with an existing risk group. Generate blocks run after membership resolution, so membership rules cannot match generated groups.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
Risk group references are validated at scenario load time:

Undefined Reference Detection: All risk group names referenced by nodes and links must exist in the risk_groups section. This catches typos and missing definitions early:

# This will fail validation
network:
  nodes:
    Router1:
      risk_groups: ["PowerZone_A"]  # References undefined risk group

risk_groups:
  - name: "PowerZone_B"  # Only PowerZone_B is defined

Circular Hierarchy Detection: Parent-child relationships cannot form cycles:

# This will fail validation
risk_groups:
  - name: "GroupA"
    children:
      - name: "GroupB"
  - name: "GroupB"
    children:
      - name: "GroupA"  # Error: circular reference

Membership follows nested descendants at any depth, including groups with no top-level entry and parent-child links added by membership rules with scope: risk_group, and a cycle among them is refused. A loop through groups declared only inline (A → B → C → B) is refused too, as a conflicting declaration of the repeated name. A group's node members and link members are kept apart, so a node name and a link id that happen to be equal never stand for each other.

Error messages name the affected entities and the undefined groups.

docs.title: vars - YAML Anchors
docs.text:
Reusable values through YAML anchors (&name) and aliases (*name):

vars:
  default_cap: &cap 10000
  base_attrs: &attrs {cost: 100, region: "dc1"}
  spine_config: &spine_cfg
    hardware:
      component: "SpineRouter"
      count: 1
    power_budget: 2500

network:
  nodes:
    spine-1: {attrs: {<<: *attrs, <<: *spine_cfg, capacity: *cap}}
    spine-2: {attrs: {<<: *attrs, <<: *spine_cfg, capacity: *cap, region: "dc2"}}

Anchor Types:

  • Scalar: &cap 10000 - Reference primitive values
  • Mapping: &attrs {cost: 100} - Reference objects
  • Merge: <<: *attrs - Merge a mapping; explicit keys win

Processing Behavior:

  • Anchors are resolved during YAML parsing, before schema validation
  • The vars section itself is ignored by NetGraph runtime logic
  • Anchors can be defined in any section, not just vars
  • Merge semantics (as parsed by PyYAML): explicit keys override merged keys regardless of position; with repeated <<: merge keys, later merges override earlier ones, while the sequence form <<: [*a, *b] gives earlier entries precedence

docs.title: demands - Traffic Demands
docs.text:
Named demand sets, each a list of demands:

demands:
  production:
    # Simple string pattern selectors
    - source: "^servers/.*"
      target: "^storage/.*"
      volume: 1000
      mode: "combine"
      priority: 1
      preset: "SHORTEST_PATHS_ECMP"

    # Dict selectors with attribute-based grouping
    - source:
        group_by: "dc"           # Group nodes by datacenter attribute
      target:
        group_by: "dc"
      volume: 500
      mode: "pairwise"
      group_mode: "group_pairwise"  # Node pairs between different datacenters
      priority: 2

    # Dict selectors with filtering
    - source:
        path: "^dc1/.*"
        match:
          conditions:
            - attr: "role"
              op: "=="
              value: "leaf"
      target:
        path: "^dc2/.*"
        match:
          conditions:
            - attr: "role"
              op: "=="
              value: "spine"
      volume: 200
      mode: "combine"

docs.title: Variable Expansion in Demands
docs.text:
Use an expand block to generate multiple demands from a template:

demands:
  inter_dc:
    - source: "^${src_dc}/.*"
      target: "^${dst_dc}/.*"
      volume: 100
      mode: "combine"
      expand:
        vars:
          src_dc: ["dc1", "dc2"]
          dst_dc: ["dc3", "dc4"]
        mode: "cartesian"  # All 4 combinations (the default)

    - source: "^${dc}/leaf/.*"
      target: "^${dc}/spine/.*"
      volume: 50
      mode: "pairwise"
      expand:
        vars:
          dc: ["dc1", "dc2", "dc3"]
        mode: "zip"        # 3 demands, paired by index

Expansion Modes:

  • cartesian: All combinations of variable values (default)
  • zip: Pair values by index (lists must have equal length)

docs.title: Demand Fields
docs.text:
Field Type Description source string or selector Source node selector (required) target string or selector Target node selector (required) volume number The declaration's total traffic, a physical amount (default: 0): the pairs and groups it expands into share it, and each expand combination has the whole total (Demands: how traffic enters) priority integer Priority class; lower = higher priority (default: 0) mode string Node pairing mode: combine or pairwise (default: combine) group_mode string How grouped nodes produce demands (default: flatten) id string Optional nonempty run-unique identity preset string Declared preset name (Presets); omission selects SHORTEST_PATHS_ECMP. Exclusive with model model object Explicit routing and admission declaration (Routing models and admission); see below attrs object Arbitrary metadata expand object Variable expansion block

A demand without an id gets <set>|<n>, where n counts the set's declarations before expansion; an expand leaf adds |<its index>, and each row adds |<its index in the expansion>. Ids are unique across the run's demand sets: a collision, declared or generated, is refused naming both.

docs.title: Named routes and explicit models
docs.text:
Named routes are declared once and compiled on the prepared graph. A Pinned model references their names in declaration order, retaining duplicates and route weights.

routes:
  via_b:
    head: A
    nodes: [A, B, C]
    weight: 3
  via_d:
    head: A
    edges:
      - {link: "A|D|0", direction: forward}
      - {link: "D|C|0", direction: forward}
    weight: 2
demands:
  traffic:
    - source: ^A$
      target: ^C$
      volume: 10
      model:
        admission: lossless
        routing: {type: pinned, routes: [via_b, via_d]}

Each route specifies its source head and exactly one of nodes, directed edges, or a named DAG support. Node paths and edge paths must be nonempty simple contiguous routes with the declared head and selected destination. A node hop takes the cheapest enabled parallel link between its two nodes, ties to the smaller link id; a disabled link in an edge path, or a node hop with no enabled link, is refused. A route is fixed when it is prepared: failures never move it.

Path routes use their declared nonnegative integer weights, default 1; a route of weight 0 is still checked in full. In converged and repair states, routes touching failed nodes or links are removed and the head splits its offer over the surviving routes by weight. In stale, the baseline program is replayed lossy at the baseline admitted total: its split stays fixed, and traffic reaching a failed element is lost there. A head with no surviving route loses its traffic. The compiled paths themselves stay fixed. Two demands with the same endpoints, model and priority stay distinct when their ids differ. Combine and pairwise are both supported when the route endpoints match the resolved question.

supports and weights are separate named namespaces:

supports:
  through_b:
    edges:
      - {link: "A|B|0", direction: forward}
      - {link: "B|C|0", direction: forward}
weights:
  explicit_split:
    entries:
      - edge: {link: "A|B|0", direction: forward}
        value: 3
